subject: chemistry
title: Organic Chemistry Adventure 2: Reactions of alkenes and alcohols
welcome_lead: Today you'll add HBr to alkenes and oxidise alcohols.
meta_desc: Chemistry — alkene addition, electrophilic addition mechanism, alcohol oxidation, Markovnikov.
final_note: You learned alkenes undergo electrophilic addition (Markovnikov gives major product), alcohols oxidise: primary → aldehyde → carboxylic acid, secondary → ketone, tertiary do not.

concepts.def: H to C with more H; major product

walkthroughs.body_html:
Alkene + HBr → bromoalkane.

Mechanism:
1. HBr polarises and Br takes pair; H⁺ adds to C=C → carbocation.
2. Br⁻ attacks carbocation.

Markovnikov: H adds to C with more Hs already → more stable carbocation gets formed → major product.

CH₃CH=CH₂ + HBr → CH₃CH(Br)CH₃ (2-bromopropane, major).

Acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ (orange → green) or KMnO₄ (purple → colourless):

Primary alcohol: distil off aldehyde, or reflux to carboxylic acid.
CH₃CH₂OH → CH₃CHO (ethanal) → CH₃COOH (ethanoic acid).

Secondary alcohol: → ketone only.
(CH₃)₂CHOH → (CH₃)₂C=O (propanone).

Tertiary alcohol: no reaction (no H on OH-carbon).

- Hydration: CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O → CH₃CH₂OH (H₃PO₄ catalyst).
- Halogenation: alkane + Cl₂ (UV) → chloroalkane via free radical chain.
- Esterification: CH₃COOH + CH₃CH₂OH ⇌ CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ + H₂O (H₂SO₄ catalyst).
- Hydrolysis: ester back to acid + alcohol.

mcqs.q: Markovnikov addition of HBr to propene gives mainly:
When HBr adds to propene, why does Br preferentially attach to the middle carbon?
options: Benzene cannot react with electrophiles at all.
Br adds to whichever carbon has more hydrogens already.
The more stable secondary carbocation forms preferentially as the intermediate, so Br adds there (Markovnikov's rule).
Br always adds to the end carbon because it's the most accessible.

mcqs.q: Why does benzene undergo electrophilic SUBSTITUTION but alkenes undergo electrophilic ADDITION?
options: Benzene cannot react with electrophiles at all.
Tertiary halogenoalkanes react via SN2 because they have more bonds to break.
Benzene reacts the same way as alkenes — by addition across one of its double bonds.
Substitution preserves benzene's stable delocalised pi system; addition would destroy aromaticity at a large energetic cost.

mcqs.q: Why do tertiary halogenoalkanes typically react via SN1 rather than SN2?
options: The tertiary carbocation intermediate is stabilised by three alkyl groups (positive inductive effect), making the SN1 pathway favourable.
Tertiary halogenoalkanes react via SN2 because they have more bonds to break.
Tertiary halogenoalkanes react via SN1 because they are more reactive in every way.
Br always adds to the end carbon because it's the most accessible.
